case_info.scenario: A 71-year-old man presented to the dermatologist with a 6-week history of a rapidly progressing rash and swelling of the left side of the chest wall. He had noticed the rash a few days after receiving the second dose of an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna). He denied itching, weeping, bleeding, or discharge from the rash or the nipple. He had a history of metabolic syndrome treated with antihypertensives and oral hypoglycemics. The physical examination showed a morbidly obese White man. The skin examination showed a 19 × 10-cm pink, fallacious purple color deep-infiltrated papule in the left breast and a similar 15 × 7-cm papule under the left clavicle (Figure, A). The breast examination was notable for bilateral gynecomastia and inverted left nipple without any palpable lumps. No lymphadenopathy was noted either. His laboratory results showed stage 2 chronic kidney disease. Results of a viral panel including hepatitis A, B, and C and HIV were negative. The punch biopsy of the skin showed a diffuse island of atypical cells in the dermis (Figure, B). On immunohistochemical staining, the atypical cells stained positive for CK-7, GATA-3, and PAX-8 (weak focal staining) and negative for estrogen receptor (ER)/progesterone receptor (<1%), TTF-1, SATB-2, CDX-2, and NKX-3.1. The positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed a diffuse, infiltrating fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid cutaneous lesion on the left chest wall (standardized uptake value, 6.5) and multiple FDG-avid nodes in the axilla (bilaterally), left internal mammary, and left cervical chain. The core biopsy from the lymph node is shown in theFigure, C.
case_info.caption: A, Rash on the left chest wall. B and C, Hematoxylin-eosin stains of the punch biopsy of the skin and core biopsy of the lymph node, respectively (both original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

4. Frustration
   Definition:

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.caption: A, Rash on the left chest wall. B and C, Hematoxylin-eosin stains of the punch biopsy of the skin and core biopsy of the lymph node, respectively (both original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 71-year-old man presented to the dermatologist with a 6-week history of a rapidly progressing rash and swelling of the left side of the chest wall. case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.
